blocks.raw:
<Callout>
Modernism evolved through distinct movements, each responding to previous aesthetics and technological shifts. Understanding the theoretical foundations—what each movement valued, rejected, and prioritized—is crucial for LEA questions on style identification and conceptual frameworks. This sequence reveals how architectural thinking transformed from craft-centered ideals to digital abstraction.
</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Test yourself on this sequence: Arts & Crafts → Art Nouveau → International Style → Brutalism → Postmodernism → Deconstructivism → Parametricism. Each movement is a *reaction against* AND *synthesis of* prior movements. Understanding these genealogies (not memorizing style names) is testable. Example: Brutalism reacts against International Style glass-box minimalism but inherits its modernist purity; it reintroduces material expression while maintaining structural logic.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>Arts and Crafts is *not* modernism—it's pre-modern philosophically (against mechanization). Yet it IS modernist aesthetically (rejecting ornament, emphasizing geometry, valuing honesty). This paradox is crucial: Arts and Crafts wanted handcrafted authenticity *in forms that modernism would later industrialize*. Modernism inherits A&C's formal vocabulary while inverting its craft ideology—the ultimate irony.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Common error: treating Mackintosh as an early modernist. He's not. Mackintosh's linear forms and surface patterns are Art Nouveau (biomimetic, ornamental) not modernist (geometric, plain). He's preface to modernism, not modernism itself. This distinction—where does one movement end and next begin?—is exactly the kind of nuanced question the LEA tests.</Warn>
